names.name: Vajradhara / Vajrasattva (the sixth buddha, lord of all families)
bodhicitta (ultimate: the union of emptiness and compassion)

descriptions: the non-duality of emptiness (prajñā) and compassion/means (upāya), 'the union of the two'
bodhicitta 'without beginning or end, beyond existence and non-existence' (Guhyasamāja ch. 2)
without beginning or end, the primordial buddha, gnosis as its sole eye (Nāmasaṃgīti 100)
negations: neither being nor non-being; 'in the absence of being there is no meditation' (Guhyasamāja 2.3)
unborn, not an object of thought or speech (the dohās)
relation_to_self: The deity one arises as is the practitioner's own purified nature ('I am Vajrasattva', vajrātmako 'ham, Tattvasaṃgraha); this 'divine pride' rests on emptiness and is not an eternal self.
relation_to_world: Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two (Pañcakrama 5.2); the world is seen as maṇḍala and deity (pure vision); ordinary appearances are the illusory display of the deity.
caveat: The Vajrayāna speaks of one non-dual gnosis (and personifies it as Vajradhara or the Ādibuddha), but always as empty of own-being; it rejects any reading of this as a permanent self or creator (Hevajra and Kālacakra commentators explicitly deny that the Ādibuddha is an Īśvara).

names.name: sahaja (lhan cig skyes pa, the innate / co-emergent)

descriptions: mind itself alone is the seed of everything, from which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa radiate; it grants what is wished like a wish-fulfilling jewel (People Dohā v42–43)
the innate is the Buddha dwelling in the body (People Dohā v82)
like space: beyond colour and shape, unstained by good and evil (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v11)
negations: not thing and not no-thing (People Dohā v21–22)
cannot be told in words (People Dohā v39)
relation_to_self: The innate is realized when self and other are not distinguished (People Dohā v73, v98); Saraha's 'self' (bdag nyid) language is not an ātman doctrine but the nature of mind.
relation_to_world: Whatever is seen in front, behind and in the ten directions is 'that itself' (People Dohā v29); saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two (People Dohā v122).
caveat: The siddhas point to the nature of mind rather than to a being; their 'one' is the non-duality of appearance and emptiness, and they would reject both an eternal self and a mere nothingness.

descriptions: the union where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two truths, grasped and grasper become one (Pañcakrama 5.2–13)
negations: 'unborn' and other such words only point to non-dual gnosis (Pañcakrama 5.27)
relation_to_self: The self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) body is the conventional truth, the illusory body of the yogin himself.
relation_to_world: The world is not self-arisen; its cause is clear light (Pañcakrama 3.15).
caveat: Clear light is 'all-empty' and non-dual gnosis — the tradition frames it within the two truths of Madhyamaka and would not accept it as a self-existent absolute.

descriptions: the gnosis that is the nature of the deity, realized by the union of the two stages
relation_to_self: The practitioner generates himself as Mañjuvajra; the deity is the purified nature.
relation_to_world: Appearances are the display of gnosis (maṇḍala).
caveat: Reconstructed from general knowledge of the school; no Jñānapāda text read locally.

descriptions: the union of Heruka (means, bliss) and Vajravārāhī (wisdom, emptiness)
the supreme bliss (śrīcakrasaṃvara) that is the 'binding' of the wheel of all phenomena
relation_to_self: The yogin's body is the maṇḍala: the twenty-four sites are its channels and the deities reside in it (body maṇḍala).
relation_to_world: The land of India (the pīṭhas) is the outer maṇḍala; worlds and bodies correspond.
caveat: The etymology 'saṃvara = supreme bliss' is the commentators'; the tradition keeps Heruka empty of own-being and distinguishes him from Śaiva Bhairava, whom he is said to have subdued.

names.name: Kālacakra (time and wheel = means and wisdom)

descriptions: the image arisen from emptiness is the cause; the bliss born of the immutable is the result; each seals the other (Sekoddeśa 146)
the fourth consecration is the ultimate, the other three are conventional (Sekoddeśa 8)
negations: the stain of mind is neither adventitious nor long-lasting, neither born without mind nor abiding in it (Sekoddeśa 129)
relation_to_self: Kālacakra is the non-dual union within the practitioner's body of the unchanging bliss and the empty form of the deity.
relation_to_world: Outer (cosmos, time), inner (body) and alternative (deity) wheels correspond; the practitioner reverses the movement of time in the channels.
caveat: The Vimalaprabhā insists that the Ādibuddha is not a creator god and not a self; it is emptiness endowed with all aspects.
